headlines: Inflation fears on the rise as one-year outlook in Fed survey hits highest level since May 2023
These 7 major S&P 500 stocks need to rally at least 200% to reclaim their peaks
Michigan’s Mike Rogers says trade war with Canada needs to end
Senate Democrats probe former Trump official’s connections to oil company
Most say Trump, Congress not taking AI risk seriously: Survey

cards.hearing: You may hear that people are expecting prices to run hotter over the next year, based on a survey the Fed, which sets short-term interest rates, keeps an eye on.
cards.why: When folks expect higher prices, it can shape real life, like how much people ask for raises or how businesses price things like groceries and rent.
cards.but: But a survey is a mood check, not a forecast carved in stone, and moods shift.
cards.story: Picture checking tomorrow's weather app and packing an umbrella just in case. Sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not, but you still go about your day. One survey reading is that umbrella, not the whole season.
say: We watch the mood, but we build your plan for the whole season, not one forecast.
A survey can shift next month. Your plan is built to handle either way.

cards.hearing: You may hear talk about the trade fight with Canada and whether it needs to end.
cards.why: Tariffs between two close trading partners can show up in costs here at home, things like lumber, cars, and even groceries that cross the border.
cards.but: But trade disputes have a long history of rising and falling, and policies shift more than once before anything is final.
cards.story: Think of two neighbors arguing over a fence line. They might argue for months, but eventually they work it out, and life on the street goes on. Meanwhile, the smart neighbor keeps tending their own garden instead of staring at the fence.
say: We keep tending your plan while the two sides sort out the fence.
Headlines like this move slowly. Your plan doesn't have to react to every update.

cards.hearing: You may hear that stocks drifted a little lower this morning after a calm rise yesterday.
cards.why: Small morning wiggles usually mean investors are digesting news, not making a big new decision about the economy.
cards.but: But a quiet dip after a quiet gain is normal, and it's not something that should change a long-term plan.
cards.story: Picture the tide at the beach. It goes out a little, then comes back in, over and over, all day long. Nobody redraws the map of the coastline because of one wave.
say: This is one wave, not a new tide.
We watch the plan, not the minute-by-minute wiggle.
